newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Chapman's racer for the road turns 40.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Chapman's racer for the road turns 40.

text.p: Forty years ago British engineer Colin Chapman's Lotus car company produced a racer that motorsport enthusiasts could use on the roads during the week and compete with on the track at weekends.
That car, the Lotus Seven, was a revelation and has been in continuous production ever since, attaining cult status among just about anybody who has ever driven it.
It is now called the Caterham 7, after the Lotus dealership which bought the rights to build it in 1973 when Lotus wanted to go up-market.
And it is easy to see why Lotus might have wanted to tempt customers with something less stark after building the Lotus Seven. It is about as minimalist as a car can get without being a motor cycle.

Looking like a spidery 1950s racing car, it is light enough to be wheeled around by hand, it doesn't have doors, you can virtually forget about the roof and there is no provision for installing a stereo system.
The in-car entertainment is provided by acceleration and handling that leave all but the most expensive supercars standing.

For those who find it too easy just to go out and buy a car, the Seven is still offered in kit form for home assembly, which takes about 70 hours and is said by the company to be "relatively idiot-proof".
Parsimonious British buyers usually opt for self-assembly while foreign owners tend to order theirs fully built by the factory, at extra cost.
The cheapest Seven is 8,995 pounds ($14,600) and the most expensive and high-powered 37,000, but few models exceed 19,000.
"The original concept was a usable road car that doubled as a weekend racer -- basic and built down to a price," said Caterham Cars Technical Director Jez Coates.
"We've tried to stay true to those values throughout all the changes we have been through."
Although the current Seven looks the same as the original 1957 model, the only parts they have in common are the rubber engine mountings.
SPECIAL ANNIVERSARY MODEL
For the 40th anniversary, Caterham are producing a special anniversary model in ruby red metallic paint with a grey stripe down the middle.

People who have never driven one dismiss the Seven as a kit-car cobbled together from the leftovers from mainstream manufacturers' parts bins. Those who have, return feeling like Mr Toad after his first experience of the motor car.
Owners become part of a semi-secret freemasonry, guiltily enjoying driving their cars in an era of spreading environmentalism.

To the uninitiated they appear to be driving around in an oversized toy. But owners know the Seven will see off just about anything short of a top-of-the-range Porsche or Ferrari, which can cost at least five times as much.
Drivers use unofficial Internet websites to swap information about where to find the right roads to get the best out of their cars without getting into trouble with the law.
Others spend weekends as the late Colin Chapman intended -- sprinting up hills or around circuits with fellow race enthusiasts.

The car's cult status was assured early on when actor Patrick McGoohan drove one through the streets of central London in the title sequence of the British 1960s spy thriller television series "The Prisoner".
The late Graham Hill began a career that led to the world drivers' championship racing Lotus Sevens in 1958.
The Seven is nowadays a big favourite with the Japanese, said Coates.
"They like it because it's traditional and British. It has the same sort of appeal as the Mini, which is a design classic. It has very high status in Japan," he said.
The Seven is the product of a very British niche in the car building business -- small companies producing distinctive, made-to-measure sports cars in limited numbers.
Best known are Morgan, TVR, Marcos, AC and Westfield, while most of the major Formula One racing teams are also scattered around the English countryside.
"I think it's a peculiarly British thing," said Coates.
"Small-scale manufacturing of engineering products is what we are good at. We are not so good at mass production."
Caterham has never produced more than 750 cars a year and has no plans to get much bigger.
"We've got no ambitions to rule the world," said Coates. "We'd like to build about 1,000 cars a year. We are a conservative company."
Growth will probably come from the Caterham 21, a new model that sports a most unCaterham-like feature -- a fully enclosed body.
There are no plans to stop making the Seven, which Coates believes can be more or less continuously refined despite its age.
One of the latest variations is the Superlight, a Seven model where much of the performance tuning is achieved by removing as much weight as possible.
The list of options available for the car is published with the weight penalty that each item imposes.
A windscreen and wipers will add 6.6 kilos (14 lb) to the 470 kilo weight of the car and a heater will put it up by a further 3.9 kilos.
And if drivers insist on carrying a spare wheel, that will slow them down by adding another 11.5 kilos to the all-up weight.
Celebrations of the 40th anniversary of the Seven are perhaps a little muted, but the company has its reasons.
"We'll push the boat out at 50 years," said Coates. "We fully expect to be here then." ($ = 0.613 British Pounds)
